claim: Viral infection at the single-cell level is highly heterogeneous, with most infected cells giving rise to no or few viral progeny while some cells produce thousands.
source: Viral infection is usually studied at the population level by averaging over millions of cells. However, infection at the single-cell level is highly heterogeneous, with most infected cells giving rise to no or few viral progeny while some cells produce thousands.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation in the abstract, supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: Population-averaged measurements of HSV-1 infection have produced contradictory results, such as the concurrent activation and inhibition of type I interferon signaling during infection.
source: Analysis of Herpes Simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection by population-averaged measurements has taught us a lot about the course of viral infection, but has also produced contradictory results, such as the concurrent activation and inhibition of type I interferon signaling during infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature showing both activation and inhibition of type I IFN pathway in the introduction section.

claim: Anti-viral signaling is initiated in a rare group of abortively infected cells during HSV-1 infection.
source: We find that anti-viral signaling is initiated in a rare group of abortively infected cells, while highly infected cells undergo cellular reprogramming to an embryonic-like transcriptional state.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by scRNA-seq data, FACS-sorted cell sequencing, and IRF3 immunofluorescence staining shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Highly infected cells undergo cellular reprogramming to an embryonic-like transcriptional state during HSV-1 infection.
source: We find that anti-viral signaling is initiated in a rare group of abortively infected cells, while highly infected cells undergo cellular reprogramming to an embryonic-like transcriptional state.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data showing upregulation of developmental genes and pathways in highly infected cells (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: β-catenin is recruited to the host nucleus and viral replication compartments during HSV-1 infection.
source: This reprogramming involves the recruitment of β-catenin to the host nucleus and viral replication compartments, and is required for late viral gene expression and progeny production.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: β-catenin recruitment is required for late viral gene expression and progeny production during HSV-1 infection.
source: This reprogramming involves the recruitment of β-catenin to the host nucleus and viral replication compartments, and is required for late viral gene expression and progeny production.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using β-catenin inhibitor iCRT14 and siRNA knockdown shown in Figure 7.

claim: Early studies in the 1940s found that bacterial burst size spans three orders of magnitude and cannot be solely attributed to differences in bacteria size.
source: For example, early studies in the 1940 s investigated the burst size of individually infected bacteria and concluded that it both spans three orders of magnitude and cannot be solely attributed to differences in bacteria size (Delbrück, 1945).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Delbrück, 1945.

claim: Many HSV-1 infected HeLa cells did not release viral progeny, and the variability between individual cells was high and did not correlate with the multiplicity of infection (MOI) used.
source: A later study measured the burst size from individual HeLa cells infected with Herpes Simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) and found that many of the infected cells did not release viral progeny, that the variability between individual cells was high and that it did not correlate with the multiplicity of infection (MOI) used (Wildy et al., 1959).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wildy et al., 1959.

claim: Technological improvements have allowed the quantification of burst sizes and determination of infection kinetics of different mammalian viruses, pointing to a high degree of cell-to-cell variability in infection.
source: More recently, technological improvements have allowed the quantification of burst sizes and determination of the infection kinetics of different mammalian viruses, pointing to a high degree of cell-to-cell variability in infection (Zhu et al., 2009; Timm and Yin, 2012; Schulte and Andino, 2014; Combe et al., 2015; Heldt et al., 2015; Cohen and Kobiler, 2016; Guo et al., 2017; Drayman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: One source of variability in viral infection is the random distribution of the number of viruses that individual cells encounter.
source: One well-known source of this variability is the random distribution of the number of viruses that individual cells encounter (Parker, 1938; Smith, 1968; Cohen and Kobiler, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parker, 1938; Smith, 1968; Cohen and Kobiler, 2016.

claim: Genetic variability in the virus population is a source of infection variability, with some virus particles being unable or less fit to establish infection.
source: Another source is genetic variability in the virus population, with some virus particles being unable or less fit to establish infection (Huang and Baltimore, 1970; Lauring et al., 2013; Stern et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Huang and Baltimore, 1970; Lauring et al., 2013; Stern et al., 2014.

claim: Host cell state at the time of infection is a source of variability among individually infected cells.
source: It is becoming clear that a third source of variability among individually infected cells is the host cell state at the time of infection (Snijder et al., 2009; Snijder et al., 2012; Drayman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Snijder et al., 2009; Snijder et al., 2012; Drayman et al., 2017.

claim: Variability in host cell state can arise from both deterministic processes, such as the cell-cycle, and stochastic processes, such as mRNA transcription and protein translation.
source: Variability in the host cell state can arise from both deterministic processes, such as the cell-cycle, and stochastic processes, such as mRNA transcription and protein translation (Elowitz et al., 2002; Cohen et al., 2008; Tay et al., 2010; Loewer and Lahav, 2011; Kellogg and Tay, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elowitz et al., 2002; Cohen et al., 2008; Tay et al., 2010; Loewer and Lahav, 2011; Kellogg and Tay, 2015.

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing has allowed researchers to examine virus–host interactions in multiple systems, mainly those of RNA viruses, highlighting extreme cell-to-cell variability during viral infection.
source: Recently, the advent of single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) has allowed researchers to examine virus–host interactions in multiple systems, mainly those of RNA viruses, highlighting the extreme cell-to-cell variability during viral infection (Steuerman et al., 2018; Russell et al., 2018a; Xin et al., 2018; Zanini et al., 2018; Shnayder et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Steuerman et al., 2018; Russell et al., 2018a; Xin et al., 2018; Zanini et al., 2018; Shnayder et al., 2018.

claim: HSV-1 is a common human pathogen that belongs to the herpesviridae family and serves as the prototypic virus for studying alpha herpesviruses infection.
source: HSV-1 is a common human pathogen that belongs to the herpesviridae family and serves as the prototypic virus for studying alpha herpesviruses infection.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HSV-1.

claim: De novo HSV-1 infection has both lytic and latent phases.
source: De novo HSV-1 infection has both lytic and latent phases.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HSV-1 infection.

claim: In the lytic phase, HSV-1 infects epithelial cells at the site of contact, replicates within these host cells, before destroying them and releasing viral progeny.
source: In the lytic phase, the virus infects epithelial cells at the site of contact, replicates withing these host cells, before destroying them and releasing viral progeny.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HSV-1 lytic infection.

claim: The latent phase of HSV-1 is restricted to neurons, in which the virus remains silent throughout the host life with occasional reactivation.
source: The latent phase is restricted to neurons, in which the virus remains silent throughout the host life with occasional reactivation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HSV-1 latent infection.

claim: Lytic HSV-1 infection is usually asymptomatic, but in some cases (particularly in immune-compromised individuals and infants), it can result in life-threatening conditions such as meningitis and encephalitis.
source: Lytic infection is usually asymptomatic, but in some cases (particularly in immune-compromised individuals and infants), it can result in life-threatening conditions such as meningitis and encephalitis.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about HSV-1 infection outcomes.

claim: To initiate infection, HSV-1 must bind to its receptors, enter the cytoplasm, travel to the nuclear pore and inject its linear double-stranded DNA into the host nucleus.
source: To initiate infection, HSV-1 must bind to its receptors, enter the cytoplasm, travel to the nuclear pore and inject its linear double-stranded DNA into the host nucleus (Kobiler et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kobiler et al., 2012.

claim: HSV-1 viral gene expression proceeds in a temporal cascade involving three classes of viral genes: immediate-early (IE), early (E) and late (L).
source: Once in the nucleus, viral gene expression proceeds in a temporal cascade involving three classes of viral genes: immediate-early (IE), early (E) and late (L) (Honess and Roizman, 1974; Honess and Roizman, 1975; Harkness et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Honess and Roizman, 1974; Honess and Roizman, 1975; Harkness et al., 2014.

claim: Transcription of HSV-1 IE genes is initiated by VP16.
source: Transcription of IE genes is initiated by VP16 (Weir, 2001), whereas transcription of the E and L genes is activated by the IE protein ICP4 (Dixon and Schaffer, 1980; Watson and Clements, 1980; DeLuca et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weir, 2001.

claim: Transcription of HSV-1 E and L genes is activated by the IE protein ICP4.
source: Transcription of IE genes is initiated by VP16 (Weir, 2001), whereas transcription of the E and L genes is activated by the IE protein ICP4 (Dixon and Schaffer, 1980; Watson and Clements, 1980; DeLuca et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dixon and Schaffer, 1980; Watson and Clements, 1980; DeLuca et al., 1985.

claim: ICP0 is a multifunctional E3-ubiquitin ligase that counteracts some of the host anti-viral systems.
source: ICP0, another IE gene, is a multifunctional E3-ubiquitn ligase that counteracts some of the host anti-viral systems (Lanfranca et al., 2014) and interferes with the action of transcriptional repressors (Gu et al., 2005; Lomonte et al., 2004; Lutz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lanfranca et al., 2014.

claim: ICP0 interferes with the action of transcriptional repressors.
source: ICP0, another IE gene, is a multifunctional E3-ubiquitn ligase that counteracts some of the host anti-viral systems (Lanfranca et al., 2014) and interferes with the action of transcriptional repressors (Gu et al., 2005; Lomonte et al., 2004; Lutz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gu et al., 2005; Lomonte et al., 2004; Lutz et al., 2017.

claim: Viral mutants that lack ICP0 expression (ΔICP0) are highly attenuated in a variety of cell types.
source: Viral mutants that lack ICP0 expression (ΔICP0) are highly attenuated in a variety of cell types (Stow and Stow, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stow and Stow, 1986.

claim: Viral DNA replication occurs in sub-nuclear structures called replication compartments (RCs) that aggregate the seven essential replication proteins as well as other viral and host proteins.
source: Viral DNA replication occurs in sub-nuclear structures, called replication compartments (RCs), that aggregate the seven essential replication proteins as well as other viral and host proteins (de Bruyn Kops and Knipe, 1988; Liptak et al., 1996; Weller and Coen, 2012; Dembowski and DeLuca, 2015; Dembowski et al., 2017; Reyes et al., 2017; Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Bruyn Kops and Knipe, 1988; Liptak et al., 1996; Weller and Coen, 2012; Dembowski and DeLuca, 2015; Dembowski et al., 2017; Reyes et al., 2017; Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018.

claim: Upon viral DNA replication, ICP4 is predominantly localized in the RCs, with some diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic localization.
source: Upon viral DNA replication, ICP4 is predominantly localized in the RCs, with some diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic localization (Knipe et al., 1987; Zhu and Schaffer, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knipe et al., 1987; Zhu and Schaffer, 1995.

claim: RNA sequencing revealed a widespread deregulation of host transcription during HSV-1 infection, including the disruption of transcription termination.
source: RNA sequencing revealed a widespread deregulation of host transcription, including the disruption of transcription termination (Rutkowski et al., 2015; Hennig et al., 2018), activation of anti-sense transcription (Wyler et al., 2017), depletion of RNA-polymerase II from the majority of host genes (Abrisch et al., 2015; Birkenheuer et al., 2018) and changes in splicing and polyadenylation (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rutkowski et al., 2015; Hennig et al., 2018.

claim: HSV-1 infection causes activation of anti-sense transcription.
source: RNA sequencing revealed a widespread deregulation of host transcription, including the disruption of transcription termination (Rutkowski et al., 2015; Hennig et al., 2018), activation of anti-sense transcription (Wyler et al., 2017), depletion of RNA-polymerase II from the majority of host genes (Abrisch et al., 2015; Birkenheuer et al., 2018) and changes in splicing and polyadenylation (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wyler et al., 2017.

claim: HSV-1 infection causes depletion of RNA-polymerase II from the majority of host genes.
source: RNA sequencing revealed a widespread deregulation of host transcription, including the disruption of transcription termination (Rutkowski et al., 2015; Hennig et al., 2018), activation of anti-sense transcription (Wyler et al., 2017), depletion of RNA-polymerase II from the majority of host genes (Abrisch et al., 2015; Birkenheuer et al., 2018) and changes in splicing and polyadenylation (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abrisch et al., 2015; Birkenheuer et al., 2018.

claim: HSV-1 infection causes changes in splicing and polyadenylation.
source: RNA sequencing revealed a widespread deregulation of host transcription, including the disruption of transcription termination (Rutkowski et al., 2015; Hennig et al., 2018), activation of anti-sense transcription (Wyler et al., 2017), depletion of RNA-polymerase II from the majority of host genes (Abrisch et al., 2015; Birkenheuer et al., 2018) and changes in splicing and polyadenylation (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2016.

claim: Although most cellular genes are downregulated by HSV-1 infection, some genes have been reported to be upregulated, including some anti-viral genes and genes encoding host transcription factors.
source: Although most cellular genes are downregulated by infection, some genes have been reported to be upregulated, including some anti-viral genes and genes encoding host transcription factors (Pasieka et al., 2006; Taddeo et al., 2002; Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pasieka et al., 2006; Taddeo et al., 2002; Hu et al., 2016.

claim: Proteomics studies have defined the different stages and protein complexes that are present during HSV-1 replication.
source: Proteomics studies have defined the different stages and protein complexes that are present during HSV-1 replication (Dembowski and DeLuca, 2015; Suk and Knipe, 2015; Dembowski et al., 2017; Reyes et al., 2017; Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018), as well as the cellular protein response to infection (Kulej et al., 2017; Lum et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dembowski and DeLuca, 2015; Suk and Knipe, 2015; Dembowski et al., 2017; Reyes et al., 2017; Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018.

claim: Proteomics studies have characterized the cellular protein response to HSV-1 infection.
source: Proteomics studies have defined the different stages and protein complexes that are present during HSV-1 replication (Dembowski and DeLuca, 2015; Suk and Knipe, 2015; Dembowski et al., 2017; Reyes et al., 2017; Dembowski and DeLuca, 2018), as well as the cellular protein response to infection (Kulej et al., 2017; Lum et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kulej et al., 2017; Lum et al., 2018.

claim: Population-level analyses of viral infection suffer from averaging over all cells in the population, which could contain opposite phenotypes leading to contradictory results.
source: Although incredibly informative, population-level analyses suffer in that they average over all the cells in the population. In the case of virus-infected cells, the population is far from homogenous and could in fact contain opposite phenotypes, such as highly- infected and abortively infected cells, leading to contradictory results.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim supported by the study's findings and general understanding of population-level measurements.

claim: Wildtype HSV-1 infection both activates and represses the type I IFN pathway according to population-level measurements.
source: The picture that emerges from population-level measurements is paradoxical, with wildtype HSV-1 infection both clearly activating (Gianni et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016; Reinert et al., 2016) and clearly repressing (Lin et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2008; Kew et al., 2013; Johnson and Knipe, 2010; Su et al., 2016; Christensen et al., 2016; Manivanh et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2018; Chiang et al., 2018) the type I IFN pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations showing both activation and repression of type I IFN pathway.

claim: Initiation of ICP4 expression was observed to occur mostly between 1 hr and 4 hr post-infection.
source: Initiation of ICP4 expression was observed to occur mostly between 1 hr and 4 hr post-infection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Almost no new HSV-1 infections were observed between 4 hr and 6 hr post-infection, but two infection peaks were later seen at 8 and 11 hr.
source: Almost no new infections were observed between 4 hr and 6 hr post-infection, but two infection peaks were later seen at 8 and 11 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The infection peaks at 8 and 11 hr post-infection are probably the result of secondary infections.
source: These peaks are probably the result of secondary infections, as new viral progeny can be detected in infected cells starting at 6 hr post-infection (Pomeranz and Blaho, 2000; Ikeda et al., 2011; Drayman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the data and citations to Pomeranz and Blaho, 2000; Ikeda et al., 2011; Drayman et al., 2017.

claim: Of 1814 cells exposed to HSV-1, 996 cells (55%) were ICP4+ and 818 (45%) were ICP4– at 5 hr post-infection.
source: Of 1814 cells exposed to HSV-1, 996 cells (55%) were ICP4+ and 818 (45%) were ICP4–.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative imaging data at 5 hr post-infection.

claim: Among ICP4+ cells, nuclear levels of ICP4 varied by ~100 fold, ranging from 7 × 10^4 to 9 × 10^6 AU.
source: Among the ICP4+ cells, nuclear levels of ICP4 varied by ~100 fold, ranging from 7 × 104 to 9 × 106 AU (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Infected cells showed three distinct phenotypes related to ICP4 localization: diffuse nuclear, discrete nuclear foci (replication compartments), and cytoplasmic foci.
source: Infected cells showed three distinct phenotypes related to ICP4 localization (Figure 1D). Upon its expression, ICP4 is initially diffuse throughout the cell nucleus. As its level increases, ICP4 forms discrete foci in the nucleus. These are the viral RCs, where viral DNA replication takes place. Later, the levels of cytoplasmic ICP4 increase and interspersed foci can be seen in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ICP4 localization phenotypes are temporally linked and delineate the progression through infection.
source: These phenotypes are temporally linked and delineate the progression through infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1—Video 1.

claim: Only 0.4% of mock-infected cells had any reads aligned to the HSV-1 genome, with a maximal expression of two viral gene counts (0.05% of transcripts).
source: Only 0.4% of mock-infected cells had any reads aligned to the HSV-1 genome, with a maximal expression of two viral gene counts (0.05% of transcripts).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data.

claim: Cells infected with either wt or ΔICP0 HSV-1 showed extreme cell-to-cell variability in the amount of viral transcripts expressed, ranging from 0–36%.
source: Cells that were infected with either wt or ΔICP0 HSV-1 showed extreme cell-to-cell variability in the amount of viral transcripts that they expressed, ranging from 0–36% (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The viral gene expression distribution was highly skewed, with most cells expressing low levels of viral transcripts and some cells expressing much higher levels.
source: The viral gene expression distribution was highly skewed, with most cells expressing low levels of viral transcripts and some cells expressing much higher levels (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The Gini coefficient for wildtype HSV-1 infection was 0.8.
source: The Gini coefficients were 0.8 for wildtype infection and 0.77 for ΔICP0 infection, higher than that reported for viral gene expression by an influenza virus (0.64; Russell et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation from scRNA-seq data.

claim: The Gini coefficient for ΔICP0 HSV-1 infection was 0.77.
source: The Gini coefficients were 0.8 for wildtype infection and 0.77 for ΔICP0 infection, higher than that reported for viral gene expression by an influenza virus (0.64; Russell et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by calculation from scRNA-seq data.

claim: The Gini coefficient for HSV-1 viral gene expression is higher than that reported for influenza virus (0.64).
source: The Gini coefficients were 0.8 for wildtype infection and 0.77 for ΔICP0 infection, higher than that reported for viral gene expression by an influenza virus (0.64; Russell et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with data from Russell et al., 2018a.

claim: When wildtype viral gene expression is visualized in two-dimensions using tSNE, two clusters of cells can be seen, distinguished by the amount of viral gene expression (less or more than ~1%).
source: When wildtype viral gene expression is visualized in two-dimensions (using the tSNE dimensionality reduction technique; van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008), two clusters of cells can be seen, which are distinguished by the amount of viral gene expression (less or more than ~1%, Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by tSNE analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The fraction of late genes increases as total viral gene expression increases, at the expense of IE and E genes.
source: The fraction of late genes increases as total viral gene expression increases, at the expense of IE and E genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of viral gene classes in single cells shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Viral gene expression is negatively correlated with the cell-cycle score, with cells in the later parts of the cell-cycle expressing ~10-fold fewer viral genes than those in the early part of the cycle.
source: We found that viral gene expression was negatively correlated with the cell-cycle score, with cells in the later parts of the cell-cycle expressing ~10-fold fewer viral genes than those in the early part of the cycle, in agreement with our previous finding in the H1299 cell-line.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell-cycle analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Canonical anti-viral genes such as IFIT2 and IFIT3 were only detected in 2–3% of the cells from both clusters 1 and 2 in wildtype HSV-1 infection.
source: In fact, canonical anti-viral genes such as IFIT2 and IFIT3 were only detected in 2–3% of the cells from both clusters 1 and 2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The expression of canonical anti-viral genes was not significantly different between mock-infected and ICP4+ cells in wildtype HSV-1 infection.
source: In agreement with the scRNA-seq data, the expression of canonical anti-viral genes was not significantly different between mock-infected and ICP4+ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq of sorted cell populations.

claim: A small group of genes, including the anti-viral genes IFIT1 and IFIT2, were specifically upregulated in the ICP4– population during wildtype HSV-1 infection.
source: Rather, our analysis indicated that a small group of genes, including the anti-viral genes IFIT1 and IFIT2, were specifically upregulated in the ICP4– population (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq of sorted cell populations shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A rare subset of ICP4– cells (<1%) showed nuclear localization of IRF3 during wildtype HSV-1 infection.
source: In ICP4+ cells, IRF3 was blocked from entering the nucleus and concentrated in the nuclear periphery (Figure 2F), while a rare subset of ICP4– cells (<1%) showed nuclear localization of IRF3.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In ICP4+ cells infected with wildtype HSV-1, IRF3 was blocked from entering the nucleus and concentrated in the nuclear periphery.
source: In ICP4+ cells, IRF3 was blocked from entering the nucleus and concentrated in the nuclear periphery (Figure 2F), while a rare subset of ICP4– cells (<1%) showed nuclear localization of IRF3.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Wildtype HSV-1 infection efficiently blocks the induction of the anti-viral response, and the activation of anti-viral genes in population-averaged measurements is the result of anti-viral signaling elicited in a rare population of abortively infected cells.
source: We thus conclude that wildtype HSV-1 infection efficiently blocks the induction of the anti-viral response and that the activation of anti-viral genes in population-averaged measurements is the result of anti-viral signaling that is elicited in a rare population of abortively infected cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scRNA-seq, sorted cell sequencing, and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Cells infected with ΔICP0 clustered into four groups.
source: Cells infected with ΔICP0 clustered into four groups (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ~8% of ΔICP0-infected cells expressed IFIT1, MX2 or OASL (compared to none of the mock-infected cells).
source: Although the magnitude of the anti-viral response in ΔICP0-infected cells was much greater than that in the wildtype-infected cells (Figure 2), it was still only observed in a small population of cells, with ~8% of the cells expressing IFIT1, MX2 or OASL (compared to none of the mock-infected cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Anti-viral signaling was not seen in the highly infected cells of cluster 4 in ΔICP0 infection, with the exception of two cells expressing IFIT1.
source: Anti-viral signaling was not seen in the highly infected cells of cluster 4, with the exception of two cells expressing IFIT1 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: ~80 genes are significantly upregulated in ΔICP0-infected ICP4– cells compared to mock and ICP4+ cells.
source: RNA-sequencing of sorted cells that were infected with ΔICP0 identified ~80 genes that are significantly upregulated in ICP4– cells compared to mock and ICP4+ cells (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq of sorted cell populations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Although enriched in the ICP4– population, anti-viral genes are also activated in the ICP4+ population during ΔICP0 infection, albeit to a lesser extent.
source: An important difference from wildtype infection is that, although enriched in the ICP4– population, these anti-viral genes are also activated in the ICP4+ population, albeit to a lesser extent (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by QPCR validation shown in Figure 3H.

claim: A higher proportion of ΔICP0-infected cells showed nuclear IRF3 localization when compared to wildtype-infected cells.
source: The staining showed that a higher proportion of ΔICP0-infected cells showed nuclear IRF3 localization when compared to wildtype-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The majority of ΔICP0-infected cells with nuclear IRF3 were ICP4– but some ICP4+ cells also showed nuclear IRF3 staining.
source: The majority of cells with nuclear IRF3 were ICP4– but some ICP4+ cells also showed nuclear IRF3 staining.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The anti-viral program is initiated in a small subset of abortively infected cells but is blocked in highly infected cells, even in the absence of ICP0.
source: Altogether, the sequencing of both single cells and sorted cell populations, as well as immuno-fluorescence staining of IRF3, suggests that the anti-viral program is initiated in a small subset of abortively infected cells but is blocked in highly infected cells, even in the absence of ICP0.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including scRNA-seq, sorted cell sequencing, and immunofluorescence.

claim: 977 genes were significantly upregulated in wildtype ICP4+ cells as compared to both ICP4– and mock-infected cells.
source: A total of 977 genes were significantly upregulated in wildtype ICP4+ cells as compared to both ICP4– and mock-infected cells in the bulk RNA-sequencing (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq of sorted cell populations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 21 genes were significantly upregulated in highly infected single cells in the scRNA-seq.
source: In the single-cell RNA-sequencing, 21 genes were significantly upregulated in highly infected single cells (Figure 4B, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A major portion of upregulated genes in HSV-1 infected cells are associated with GO terms concerning the regulation of RNA transcription and developmental processes.
source: Remarkably, we found that a major portion of these upregulated genes are associated with GO terms that concern the regulation of RNA transcription and developmental processes (Figure 4C,D and Supplementary files 1b and 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis of upregulated genes shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The promoters of upregulated genes in HSV-1 infected cells are enriched for the binding sites of several transcription factors, including LEF1, TCF3 and MYC.
source: The promoters of these upregulated genes are enriched for the binding sites of several transcription factors, including LEF1, TCF3 and MYC (Figure 4E,F and Supplementary files 1c and 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor binding site analysis shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: 23% of the promoters of the upregulated genes in ICP4+ cells contained a binding site for the TCF/LEF transcription factors.
source: 23% of the promoters of the upregulated genes in ICP4+ cells contained a binding site for the TCF/LEF transcription factors, which are activated by the WNT/β-catenin pathway (Sokol, 2011) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcription factor binding site analysis and citation to Sokol, 2011.

claim: LEF1 itself is a WNT target gene that is upregulated during HSV-1 infection.
source: Note that LEF1 itself is a WNT target gene that is upregulated during HSV-1 infection (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Upregulated genes in HSV-1 infected cells include canonical WNT target genes such as AXIN2.
source: Examples of upregulated genes are shown in Figure 5A and include canonical WNT target genes such as AXIN2, key developmental genes belonging to the SOX, HOX and HES families, stem-cell associated transcripts such as LGR5, and a multitude of extra-cellular ligands of various developmental pathways, including the WNT, Notch, Hedgehog and TGFβ signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Upregulated genes in HSV-1 infected cells include key developmental genes belonging to the SOX, HOX and HES families.
source: Examples of upregulated genes are shown in Figure 5A and include canonical WNT target genes such as AXIN2, key developmental genes belonging to the SOX, HOX and HES families, stem-cell associated transcripts such as LGR5, and a multitude of extra-cellular ligands of various developmental pathways, including the WNT, Notch, Hedgehog and TGFβ signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Upregulated genes in HSV-1 infected cells include stem-cell associated transcripts such as LGR5.
source: Examples of upregulated genes are shown in Figure 5A and include canonical WNT target genes such as AXIN2, key developmental genes belonging to the SOX, HOX and HES families, stem-cell associated transcripts such as LGR5, and a multitude of extra-cellular ligands of various developmental pathways, including the WNT, Notch, Hedgehog and TGFβ signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Upregulated genes in HSV-1 infected cells include extra-cellular ligands of various developmental pathways, including the WNT, Notch, Hedgehog and TGFβ signaling pathways.
source: Examples of upregulated genes are shown in Figure 5A and include canonical WNT target genes such as AXIN2, key developmental genes belonging to the SOX, HOX and HES families, stem-cell associated transcripts such as LGR5, and a multitude of extra-cellular ligands of various developmental pathways, including the WNT, Notch, Hedgehog and TGFβ signaling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Concomitant with the establishment of an embryonic-like transcriptional program, there is a reduction in the levels of key fibroblast-marker genes, such as those encoding α1(III) collagen and fibronectin.
source: Concomitant with the establishment of this embryonic-like transcriptional program, we observed a reduction in the levels of key fibroblast-marker genes, such as those encoding α1(III) collagen and fibronectin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cells that are highly infected by HSV-1 undergo de-repression of embryonic and developmental genetic programs, including the WNT/β-catenin pathway.
source: We conclude that cells that are highly infected by HSV-1 undergo de-repression of embryonic and developmental genetic programs, including the WNT/β-catenin pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data showing upregulation of developmental genes.

claim: β-catenin was mainly cytoplasmic/membrane-bound in mock-infected cells.
source: As expected, β-catenin was mainly cytoplasmic/membrane-bound in mock-infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In HSV-1-infected cells, β-catenin showed three distinct localization patterns: un-perturbed (cytoplasmic), diffuse nuclear or aggregated in nuclear foci.
source: In HSV-1-infected cells, β-catenin showed three distinct localization patterns: un-perturbed (cytoplasmic), diffuse nuclear or aggregated in nuclear foci (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: At 5 hr post-infection, 37% of the cells were ICP4 negative, 14% were at the earliest stage of infection (diffuse nuclear ICP4), 31% had assembled viral replication compartments and 18% had progressed to show cytoplasmic foci of ICP4.
source: At 5 hr post-infection, 37% of the cells were ICP4 negative, 14% were at the earliest stage of infection (diffuse nuclear ICP4), 31% had assembled viral replication compartments and 18% had progressed to show cytoplasmic foci of ICP4 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: β-catenin localization was linked to the temporal progression of HSV-1 infection.
source: β-catenin localization was linked to the temporal progression of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B,E.

claim: β-catenin remained cytoplasmic in both ICP4– cells and cells with diffused nuclear ICP4.
source: β-catenin remained cytoplasmic in both ICP4–cells and cells with diffused nuclear ICP4, translocated to the nucleus upon the generation of the replication compartments and subsequently co-localized with the RCs, but only in cells showing cytoplasmic foci of ICP4 (Figure 6B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B,E.

claim: β-catenin translocated to the nucleus upon the generation of the replication compartments.
source: β-catenin remained cytoplasmic in both ICP4–cells and cells with diffused nuclear ICP4, translocated to the nucleus upon the generation of the replication compartments and subsequently co-localized with the RCs, but only in cells showing cytoplasmic foci of ICP4 (Figure 6B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B,E.

claim: β-catenin co-localized with the RCs, but only in cells showing cytoplasmic foci of ICP4.
source: β-catenin remained cytoplasmic in both ICP4–cells and cells with diffused nuclear ICP4, translocated to the nucleus upon the generation of the replication compartments and subsequently co-localized with the RCs, but only in cells showing cytoplasmic foci of ICP4 (Figure 6B,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B,E.

claim: β-catenin is co-opted by HSV-1.
source: This analysis indicates that β-catenin is indeed co-opted by HSV-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the β-catenin localization data.

claim: Cell-to-cell variability in the progression of infection results in heterogeneity of β-catenin localization, with recruitment of β-catenin to the viral replication compartments occurring during the later stages of infection.
source: Cell-to-cell variability in the progression of infection results in heterogeneity of β-catenin localization, with recruitment of β-catenin to the viral replication compartments occurring during the later stages of infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the β-catenin localization data across different infection stages.

claim: β-catenin inhibition had no or minimal impact on immediate-early gene expression.
source: Our results indicate that β-catenin inhibition had no or minimal impact on immediate-early gene expression (Figure 7A) but significantly inhibited early and late gene expression (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: β-catenin inhibition significantly inhibited early and late viral gene expression.
source: Our results indicate that β-catenin inhibition had no or minimal impact on immediate-early gene expression (Figure 7A) but significantly inhibited early and late gene expression (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: β-catenin inhibition significantly reduced viral progeny formation.
source: In accordance with its impact on late viral gene expression, β-catenin inhibition significantly reduced viral progeny formation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: iCRT14 reduces plaque formation in HLF and Vero cell types.
source: This is in agreement with a recent report by Zhu and Jones (2018) showing iCRT14-reduced plaque formation in two other cell types (HLF and Vero).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhu and Jones, 2018.

claim: β-catenin silencing using siRNA reduced viral progeny formation.
source: Similar results were obtained when β-catenin was silenced using siRNA (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: HSV-1 reprograms the cell to an embryonic-like state, in part through the co-option of β-catenin, which is needed for late viral gene expression and progeny production.
source: Taken together, our data show that HSV-1 reprograms the cell to an embryonic-like state, in part through the co-option of β-catenin, which is needed for late viral gene expression and progeny production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined RNA-seq, immunofluorescence, and functional inhibition data.

claim: Single cells infected by HSV-1 show variability in all aspects of infection, starting from the initial phenotype (abortive infection vs. successful initiation of viral gene expression), through the timing and rate of viral gene expression and ending with the cellular response of the host cell.
source: We find that single cells tha are infected by the virus show variability in all aspects of infection, starting from the initial phenotype (abortive infection vs. successful initiation of viral gene expression), through the timing and rate of viral gene expression and ending with the cellular response of the host cell.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental data in the study.

claim: The findings uncover the transcriptional differences in cells with variable infection outcomes.
source: These findings uncover the transcriptional differences in cells with variable infection outcomes and shed new light on the manipulation of host pathways by HSV-1.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contributions.

claim: Single-cell investigations into RNA viruses such as West-Nile virus and influenza have reported rare activation of anti-viral signaling similar to HSV-1.
source: This rare activation of anti-viral signaling seems to be widespread, as single-cell investigations into RNA viruses such as West-Nile virus (O'Neal et al., 2019) and influenza (Russell et al., 2018a; Russell et al., 2018b) have reported similar findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Neal et al., 2019; Russell et al., 2018a; Russell et al., 2018b.

claim: There is a growing body of literature showing a link between viral infection and the β-catenin pathway.
source: These findings augment a growing body of literature that shows a link between viral infection and the β-catenin pathway (reviewed in van Zuylen et al., 2016), such as during infections with murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) (Juranic Lisnic et al., 2013), influenza (More et al., 2018), hepatitis B virus (HBV) (Daud et al., 2017) and Rift Valley Fever virus (Harmon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Zuylen et al., 2016; Juranic Lisnic et al., 2013; More et al., 2018; Daud et al., 2017; Harmon et al., 2016.

claim: A direct involvement of ICP0 in the massive reprogramming of the host cell state can be ruled out because this reprogramming also occurs during infection with ΔICP0, albeit to a lesser extent.
source: How HSV-1 infection causes this massive reprogramming of the host cell state is currently unknown, although we can rule out a direct involvement of ICP0 because this reprogramming also occurs during infection with ΔICP0, albeit to a lesser extent.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of wildtype and ΔICP0 infection data.

claim: A proteomics study of host chromatin during HSV-1 infection has identified widespread changes in the epigenomic landscape of infected cells.
source: Indeed, a proteomics study of host chromatin during HSV-1 infection has identified widespread changes in the epigenomic landscape of infected cells (Kulej et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kulej et al., 2017.

claim: A recent report described an inhibitory role for the germline transcription factor DUX4 during HSV-1 infection.
source: Although we describe a positive role for β-catenin activation during HSV-1 infection here, a recent report described an inhibitory role for the germline transcription factor DUX4 during HSV-1 infection (Full et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Full et al., 2019.

claim: β-catenin and other developmental pathways are often found to be mutated or dysregulated during tumorigenesis.
source: β-catenin and other developmental pathways are often found to be mutated or dysregulated during tumorigenesis (Reya and Clevers, 2005; Krausova and Korinek, 2014; Duchartre et al., 2016) and are considered to be promising targets for cancer treatment (Takebe et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reya and Clevers, 2005; Krausova and Korinek, 2014; Duchartre et al., 2016.

claim: β-catenin and other developmental pathways are considered to be promising targets for cancer treatment.
source: β-catenin and other developmental pathways are often found to be mutated or dysregulated during tumorigenesis (Reya and Clevers, 2005; Krausova and Korinek, 2014; Duchartre et al., 2016) and are considered to be promising targets for cancer treatment (Takebe et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Takebe et al., 2015.

claim: The first-line treatment for late-stage melanoma is the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
source: At present, the first-line treatment for late-stage melanoma is the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (Tracey and Vij, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tracey and Vij, 2019.

claim: Heterogeneity in response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in melanoma was shown to be associated with β-catenin activity in the tumor, where high β-catenin levels negatively correlate with treatment success.
source: This heterogeneity was shown to be associated with β-catenin activity in the tumor, where high β-catenin levels negatively correlate with treatment success (Spranger and Gajewski, 2015; Spranger et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Spranger and Gajewski, 2015; Spranger et al., 2015.

claim: An HSV-1-based oncolytic therapy has been FDA approved for late-stage melanoma.
source: Given that an HSV-1 -based oncolytic therapy has been FDA approved for late-stage melanoma (Pol et al., 2015), it is tempting to speculate that the high level of β-catenin in melanomas that are resistant to checkpoint inhibitors would serve to augment oncolytic HSV-1 replication and anti-tumor effects, although this of course would have to be assessed carefully in separate studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pol et al., 2015.

claim: The genome:PFU ratio for the wildtype HSV-1 viral stock was 36 ± 4.
source: Note that we determined the genome:PFU ratio for our viral stock and found it to be 36 ± 4, suggesting that all the cells in the culture have probably encountered numerous virus particles.
evidence: This claim is supported by digital droplet PCR measurements described in the methods.

claim: The genome:PFU ratio for ΔICP0 HSV-1 was 1,422 ± 34.
source: These measurements revealed a genomes:PFU ratio of 36 ± 4 for wildtype HSV-1 and 1,422 ± 34 for ΔICP0.
evidence: This claim is supported by digital droplet PCR measurements described in the methods.

claim: All the cells in the culture have probably encountered at least one viral genome during infection.
source: Note that, assuming a Poisson distribution, it is unlikely that any of the cells in our experiment did not encounter at least one viral genome (p=4×10−31 for wildtype and 1 × 10−304 for ΔICP0).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical calculation based on MOI and genome:PFU ratio.
